intrinsic_value_estimate: About $50 per share, within a range of $32–75. Method: owner earnings per Section 3 (1987: net income $916M + D&A $154M – capex $300M; range $2.05–2.45/share, midpoint $2.25). The 'past repeats' case grows owner earnings 12% a year (the record runs 11.2% over 10 years and 13.0% since 1981), discounts 10 years of dividends plus a 15x exit multiple at 12% (management's stated cost of capital), giving about $50; at 10% it gives about $58.5. Growth slowing to 8% gives about $32; 15% international-driven growth gives about $75. On the framework's literal net-working-capital test, value is only $0.05–0.95/share (it fails), but that test is the partnership-era bargain rule, superseded for outstanding businesses by the 1981/1987 'sensible price' standard.
margin_of_safety: Thin. Against the about $50 central value at a 12% discount rate, the margin is about 7%. At 10% it is about 20%. There is no discount to net working capital (price is 5.4x book, about 21x owner earnings, about 23x owner earnings for the core once about $6.20/share of affiliate stakes is stripped out). The framework sets no numeric hurdle. The partnership-era 'comfortable margin of safety' is not met on price alone, so the protection comes from how predictable the business is and from buybacks that add to per-share value. That is why the position is sized at about half the framework's 40% ceiling.

key_reasons.reason: High return on equity capital without relying on leverage or accounting tricks
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 3: Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: Return on average equity 21.8%/23.5%/28.8%/27.2% (1984–87); about 25% return on net capital employed in 1987 after stripping out net debt (about $581M) and after-tax net interest; 1977 return on equity of 20.6% was earned with debt at only 3.5% of capital; soft-drink segments earned about 34–36% pretax on identifiable assets.

key_reasons.reason: Wide, durable moat that management is actively widening
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 3: Durable competitive advantage, the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986)
key_reasons.evidence: About 44% of world soft-drink volume (outside USSR/China), double the nearest competitor; 39%+ US share, 59% of US fountain; US concentrate gross margin about 63%; discretionary pricing under the CCE contract; international per-person consumption only 16% of the US level; bottler consolidation (Germany 102→68 bottlers) and switch from syrup to concentrate.

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are close to reported earnings because the core needs little capital
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 3: Owner earnings (brk-letter-1986); low-capital, high-profit businesses need little debt (fortune-1977-inflation)
key_reasons.evidence: 1987 owner earnings about $770M ($2.07/share) using total capex; core soft-drink capex $170M against $103M depreciation and $1,433M operating income; capital-heavy bottling held in 49% affiliates.

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have produced far more than $1 of market value per $1 retained
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 4: Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983)
key_reasons.evidence: End 1980 → end 1987: about $4.81–5.71/share retained against a $27.00/share price gain (about $5 per $1); EPS rose from $1.14 to $2.43 on about $5.71 retained, roughly a 22% return on retained earnings.

key_reasons.reason: Large, repeated buybacks show management acts for shareholders, mostly at prices below value
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 4: Buybacks only well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1984)
key_reasons.evidence: About 50.4M shares (about 12% of the company) bought for $1.43B, 1984–87, at an average of about $28.40, well below the current $46.56; a further program of up to 40M shares runs through 1990; diversification into entertainment was unwound via the CPE spin-off.

key_reasons.reason: The price makes sense if the future looks like the past; an outstanding business at a sensible price is the goal
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 5 as applied through brk-letter-1981 ('prices that will make sense, even should the future… develop much along the lines of its past'; 'fairly fancy price for a Category 1 business') and brk-letter-1987 ('outstanding business at a sensible price, not a mediocre business at a bargain price')
key_reasons.evidence: Value about $50 (12%) to $58.5 (10%) against $46.56; about 5.2% earnings yield and about 4.4–5.3% owner-earnings yield, growing at the historical 11–13% a year.

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst needed; compounding plus buybacks will eventually show up in the price
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 6: No catalyst needed, the market eventually reflects business results (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: Steady record of growing earnings per share since 1976; 26 consecutive dividend increases; 40M-share repurchase authorization still mostly unused.

key_reasons.reason: Concentrate, but below the ceiling because the price margin is thin
key_reasons.framework_principle: Section 7: Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965)
key_reasons.evidence: Very low probability of a drastic change in value (100-year franchise, unleveraged returns of about 25%), but margin of safety only about 7–20%, no 1988 results, and growth includes currency gains (key currencies +27% in 1986, +16% in 1987).

risks: Thin margin of safety: if growth slows to about 8%, value is about $32, about 30% below the current price
Growth has been flattered by currency: international operating income gains in 1986–87 coincided with 16–27% currency appreciation; a stronger dollar would reverse it

Management's 35% net debt-to-capital target is leverage the business doesn't need; gross debt/capital is already 45.6%, plus about $394M of guarantees, $325M of CPE recourse receivables, and about $300M of finance-subsidiary debt to be consolidated in 1988
Retained cash is increasingly going into bottler stakes earning about 6% (CCE about 5.8% on carrying value) and a 49% CPE stake earning about 4% on net assets
Past capital misallocation (1982–86 entertainment diversification; 1985 issuance of about 7.1M shares for Embassy) could recur
Brand depends on heavy marketing ($720M media spend, about 28% of revenue in selling expenses); the 1985 formula change showed management can misjudge the franchise
Promotional tone of the annual reports; no first-hand assessment of management's character or insider ownership
1988 results not available; the valuation rests on the 1987 base
what_would_change_my_mind: 1988 results showing currency-neutral soft-drink volume and profit growth in the low single digits (would push weight toward the about $32 scenario)
Long-term government bond yields well above the 10–12% discount rates used, making a 4–5% owner-earnings yield unattractive
A price run-up well above about $55 without matching earnings growth, which would make the price unreasonable even for this business (would pause new buying rather than trigger a sale)
A large acquisition outside soft drinks, or share issuance on unfavorable terms
Evidence that buybacks are being made with borrowed money at prices clearly above intrinsic value
Proxy evidence of negligible insider ownership or compensation that rewards size rather than returns
Conversely, a price fall toward $35–40 with the business intact would justify adding toward the framework's higher concentration limits
sell_triggers: Evidence the moat has been misread: sustained loss of world or US share to the main competitor, or erosion of concentrate gross margin and pricing power
Unleveraged return on capital falling persistently below about 20% (the long-run level before 1984)
Net debt-to-capital pushed beyond the 35% target, or debt used to fund low-return diversification
A return to large acquisitions outside the core paid for with stock that is worth more than what is received in business value
Loss of confidence in management's integrity or candor (e.g., misleading reporting of one-off items)
Not a trigger: price alone. The default for a great business with able management is to hold permanently.
